screens.title: Adapting and Enhancing: Adapter and Decorator Patterns
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn two complementary structural patterns that help existing code keep working while your system evolves. First, the Adapter pattern solves the classic problem of incompatible interfaces: it lets client code speak the interface it expects while translating calls to an older or third-party class without modifying that class. Second, the Decorator pattern offers a runtime way to add responsibilities to individual objects, avoiding a combinatorial explosion of subclasses. You will see concrete examples: adapting a legacy payment gateway to a new payment interface and wrapping a simple coffee object with milk and sugar decorators. We'll also cover trade-offs: composition versus inheritance for adapters, and when a decorator is preferable to subclassing. These patterns are practical for integrating legacy systems, extending behavior in deployed code, and composing features at runtime. As you proceed, notice the difference in intent—Adapter changes interfaces, Decorator adds responsibilities—and try to predict which pattern fits small real-world scenarios. What integration problem in your codebase could use an adapter, and where might decorators reduce subclass complexity?

screens.title: What is the Adapter pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: The Adapter pattern is a structural design pattern whose purpose is to convert the interface of an existing class into another interface the client expects. Imagine a device plug and an outlet socket that don't match: the adapter sits between them and translates the connection. In software, the adapter accepts calls in the target interface, performs any translation or mapping, and delegates the work to the adaptee. This means you do not modify the original adaptee — a crucial advantage when that code is third-party, legacy, or widely reused. A concrete example from this chapter is adapting a legacy payment gateway that expects a legacy currency code to a new payment processor interface that uses currency abbreviations. The adapter maps the currency formats and forwards the call. A common misconception is that an adapter changes the adaptee; it does not. Another confusion is mixing adapters with proxies or decorators; adapters change interface, proxies control access, and decorators add behavior. Key takeaway: use adapters when the interface mismatch, not when you need to change behavior. How would you describe a good translation between two interfaces in your current project?

keyIdea.title: Adapter Definition
keyIdea.text: Adapter converts one interface into another so existing classes can be reused safely.

content.html:
Core Concept
Adapter pattern explained
Translate a target interface into calls the adaptee understands, without editing the adaptee.
Definition
Converts one interface into another expected by the client.
When to use
Integrating legacy or third-party code with a new system interface.
Common mistake
Modifying the adaptee instead of creating an adapter.
Key Takeaway

Adapter preserves existing implementations by translating interfaces at the boundary.

Object Adapter Example (code snippet)
# Adaptee
class OldPaymentGateway:
    def process_payment_legacy(self, amount, currency_code):
        print("Old Payment Gateway: Processing", amount, currency_code)
        return True

# Target Interface
class NewPaymentProcessor:
    def make_payment(self, amount, currency):
        raise NotImplementedError

# Adapter uses composition to wrap adaptee and translate calls to legacy format
Concrete Example
Adapter maps currency codes like USD to legacy numeric codes and delegates processing to the old gateway.
Misconception
Adapters do not add behavior; they translate interfaces. Use decorators for behavior changes.

screens.title: Object Adapter vs Class Adapter
screens.narratorSegment: There are two conceptual forms of adapters: object adapters and class adapters. An object adapter uses composition: it holds an instance of the adaptee and translates calls from the client's expected interface into calls on that internal instance. This form is the most common because it preserves encapsulation and works easily in languages that limit multiple inheritance. A class adapter uses inheritance: the adapter inherits from both the target interface and the adaptee, effectively being both. While class adapters can be concise in languages that support multiple inheritance, they break encapsulation and tightly couple the adapter to the adaptee. A concrete trade-off: object adapters let you swap or mock the adaptee at runtime and make testing easier; class adapters bake the adaptee's behavior into the adapter and are harder to change. A common misunderstanding is to assume class adapters always require language-level multiple inheritance; think of them conceptually but implement with composition when multiple inheritance is not practical. Key takeaway: prefer composition for flexibility and testability unless you have a compelling reason and language support for class adapters. Object Adapter vs Class Adapter means object adapters favor flexibility and encapsulation; class adapters can be simpler conceptually but increase coupling.. In practical terms, trade-offs between composition and inheritance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Trade-off Summary
keyIdea.text: Object adapters favor flexibility and encapsulation; class adapters can be simpler conceptually but increase coupling.

content.html:
Comparison
Object Adapter
Uses composition: adapter holds an adaptee instance and forwards translated calls.
  • Preserves encapsulation.
  • Easy to swap or mock the adaptee for testing.
  • Preferred in languages without multiple inheritance.
Key Takeaway

Composition leads to flexible, testable adapters.

Comparison
Class Adapter
Uses multiple inheritance: adapter inherits from target and adaptee conceptually, so it can be both.
  • May be concise in some languages.
  • Tight coupling to adaptee implementation.
  • Less flexible for swapping or testing the adaptee.
Misconception
Class adapters are always better because they are shorter. Not true: coupling and language support matter.

screens.title: Adapter Code Walkthrough
screens.narratorSegment: Let's walk through the object adapter example from the chapter to make the idea concrete. The client expects a NewPaymentProcessor with a make payment method that accepts an amount and a currency abbreviation such as USD. The existing class, OldPaymentGateway, exposes process payment legacy and expects an amount and a legacy numeric currency code. The adapter implements the NewPaymentProcessor interface and holds an OldPaymentGateway instance. When make payment is called, the adapter maps the readable currency abbreviation to the legacy code, perhaps using a small dictionary, and calls process payment legacy on the adaptee. This preserves the old gateway's behavior and avoids touching its source. A practical pitfall is to leak adapter mapping logic across the codebase; keep translation logic within the adapter. Another misconception is treating adapters as feature enhancers; they should focus on translation. Example: the adapter maps USD to 840 and returns whatever the adaptee returns, allowing the client to remain unaware of legacy formats. Takeaway: test adapters with both real and mocked adaptees to ensure translations are correct and edge cases like unknown currencies are handled predictably.

keyIdea.title: Implementation Pattern
keyIdea.text: Adapter implements target, holds adaptee, translates calls, and delegates.

content.html:
Process Flow
Adapter in action
# Adapter implements target and wraps adaptee
class PaymentGatewayAdapter(NewPaymentProcessor):
    def __init__(self, old_gateway):
        self._old_gateway = old_gateway

    def make_payment(self, amount, currency):
        # translate currency to legacy code and call adaptee
        currency_code_map = {"USD": "840", "EUR": "978"}
        legacy_code = currency_code_map.get(currency.upper(), "UNKNOWN")
        return self._old_gateway.process_payment_legacy(amount, legacy_code)

# Client uses adapter as if it were a NewPaymentProcessor
Concrete Example
Mapping USD to a legacy numeric code and delegating preserves the old gateway's logic while the client uses the new API.
Edge Case
Handle unknown currencies explicitly to avoid surprising the client with an adaptee failure.
Testing & Best Practices
  • Keep translation logic inside the adapter.
  • Write unit tests with mocked adaptee to verify mappings.
  • Log translation failures and return clear errors to the client.
Try this
Swap the adaptee instance at runtime to integrate a newer gateway without changing client code.

screens.title: What is the Decorator pattern?
screens.narratorSegment: The Decorator pattern is a structural pattern that lets you attach new responsibilities to objects at runtime by wrapping them in decorator objects that conform to the same interface. This approach avoids creating many specialized subclasses for each combination of features. Think of a simple coffee object that has base cost and description; rather than creating subclasses for every topping combination, you wrap the base coffee in a milk decorator, then wrap that in a sugar decorator, and so on. Each decorator delegates to its wrapped component for core behavior and augments cost or description as needed. A common misconception is that decorators are identical to proxies or adapters. While all three use wrapping, their intent differs: decorator focuses on behavior addition, adapter focuses on interface translation, and proxy focuses on controlling access. Example: adding encryption to a data source by wrapping it in an EncryptionDecorator transforms returned data without changing the underlying data source. Takeaway: use decorators when you need per-instance, composable features rather than global class-wide behavior. What is the Decorator pattern? means decorator wraps a component to add responsibilities while preserving the component's public interface.. In practical terms, add responsibilities to objects dynamically without subclassing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

keyIdea.title: Decorator Definition
keyIdea.text: Decorator wraps a component to add responsibilities while preserving the component's public interface.

content.html:
Core Concept
Decorator pattern
Wrap a component to add behavior dynamically, preserving the common interface.
  • Avoids class explosion from many feature combinations.
  • Supports per-instance feature composition at runtime.
  • Each decorator delegates then augments behavior.
Key Takeaway

Decorator composes features around objects so you can combine behavior flexibly.

Coffee Example (structure)
# Component Interface
class Coffee:
    def get_cost(self): pass
    def get_description(self): pass

# Concrete Component
class SimpleCoffee(Coffee): ...

# Decorator
class CoffeeDecorator(Coffee):
    def __init__(self, decorated):
        self._decorated = decorated

# Concrete Decorator
class MilkDecorator(CoffeeDecorator):
    def get_cost(self): return self._decorated.get_cost() + 1.5
    def get_description(self): return self._decorated.get_description() + ", with Milk"
Concrete Example
Wrap a SimpleCoffee with MilkDecorator and then SugarDecorator to build a customized drink at runtime.
Contrast
Inheritance would require one subclass per combination, which scales poorly.

screens.title: Decorator Implementation Steps
screens.narratorSegment: Designing decorators follows a practical sequence. First, define a component interface that lists the operations clients use. Second, implement one or more concrete components that provide the base behavior. Third, create an abstract decorator that implements the component interface and holds a reference to another component. This decorator forwards calls to the wrapped component. Fourth, implement concrete decorators that override or extend specific methods, delegating to the wrapped component and then adding responsibilities such as encryption, compression, or UI enhancements. A concrete example: start with a FileDataSource that reads text from a file, then create an EncryptionDecorator that wraps any DataSource, obtains its data, transforms it by reversing the string to simulate encryption, and returns the transformed text. Important practice: keep decorators single-purpose and composable so they can be layered and tested independently. A misconception to avoid is putting too much logic into a decorator; prefer multiple small decorators instead of one large one. Takeaway: follow the small, composable steps and test each decorator in isolation and in combination. Decorator Implementation Steps means define component, implement base, create abstract decorator, add small single-purpose decorators and layer them.. In practical terms, how to design and layer decorators safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow
Design and layer decorators
Step 1 — Define Component
Declare the interface clients use so decorators and components match it.
Step 2 — Implement Base
Provide a concrete component like FileDataSource that reads raw data.
Step 3 — Create Decorator
Abstract decorator holds a reference to a component and forwards calls.
Step 4 — Add Small Decorators
Implement single-purpose decorators such as encryption or compression and layer them.
Example
EncryptionDecorator reverses text returned by any DataSource to simulate encryption.
Pro Tip
Keep decorators small and composable for easier testing and reuse.
Common Mistake
Packing multiple unrelated responsibilities into one decorator makes layering fragile.

keyIdea.title: Composition Behavior
keyIdea.text: Decorators form a call chain that delegates inward and augments behavior on the return path; order matters.

content.html:
Code Walkthrough
Layering decorators
# Base
class SimpleCoffee(Coffee):
    def get_cost(self): return 5.0
    def get_description(self): return "Simple Coffee"

# Decorator
class CoffeeDecorator(Coffee):
    def __init__(self, decorated):
        self._decorated = decorated

# Concrete Decorator
class MilkDecorator(CoffeeDecorator):
    def get_cost(self): return self._decorated.get_cost() + 1.5
    def get_description(self): return self._decorated.get_description() + ", with Milk"

# Compose
c = SimpleCoffee()
c = MilkDecorator(c)
c = SugarDecorator(c)
print(c.get_cost(), c.get_description())
Concrete Example
Stack Milk then Sugar to accumulate cost; reversing order changes the output composition order.
Misconception
Decorators are not singletons; each wrapped instance can differ and be composed independently.
DataSource layering
# FileDataSource returns raw text
# EncryptionDecorator wraps a DataSource and returns reversed string
encrypted = EncryptionDecorator(FileDataSource())
print(encrypted.get_data())

# Combine with adapter
adapted = LegacyDataAdapter(LegacyDatabaseConnector())
adapted_encrypted = EncryptionDecorator(adapted)
print(adapted_encrypted.get_data())
Try this
Layer decorators in different orders and observe how composed output changes to build intuition.

screens.title: When to use Adapter vs Decorator
screens.narratorSegment: Deciding between Adapter and Decorator begins with intent. If the problem is an interface mismatch — your client expects method names or data shapes that an existing class does not provide — the Adapter pattern is the correct tool. It bridges the gap so the client can use that existing class without modification. If instead you need to add or vary functionality for particular object instances at runtime — for example adding encryption, compression, or UI features — reach for Decorator. In real scenarios: integrating a third-party payment gateway uses an adapter; adding logging or encryption to a data source uses decorators. Compare behavior: adapters change the contract shape, decorators enhance behavior. A typical pitfall is to choose inheritance to add features when only some instances need them; that creates many subclasses. Another pitfall is to wrap an adapter inside a decorator and expect the adapter to change behavior — adapters should remain focused on translation. A good rule: ask two questions — do I need to change the interface, or do I need to change the behavior of some instances? Your answers point to Adapter or Decorator respectively. Try to apply this rule in a small refactor and observe how it constrains the number of new classes you create.

keyIdea.text: Ask: change interface (Adapter) or change instance behavior (Decorator)? Use the pattern that matches the intent.

content.html:
Architecture
When to choose each pattern
Adapter — Typical Scenarios
  • Integrating legacy or third-party libraries with a new interface.
  • Refactoring to a new API while preserving old implementations.
  • Providing a compatibility layer during migration.
Decorator — Typical Scenarios
  • Adding features like encryption, compression, or UI modifiers per instance.
  • Composing responsibilities dynamically at runtime.
  • Avoiding explosion of subclasses for feature combinations.
Pro Tip
Keep adapters responsible for translation only and decorators for behavior only; mixing responsibilities creates maintenance overhead.

screens.title: Activity: Adapter for a Legacy Data Source
screens.narratorSegment: This hands-on activity asks you to implement an adapter that makes a LegacyDatabaseConnector compatible with a DataSource interface. screens.title: Activity: EncryptionDecorator for DataSource
screens.narratorSegment: In the second part of the activity you'll implement an EncryptionDecorator that wraps any DataSource and encrypts returned data before delivering it to the client. For simplicity the chapter uses string reversal to simulate encryption. The decorator should implement get data, call the wrapped DataSource's get data, perform the transformation, and return the modified string. This pattern is useful for adding cross-cutting concerns like encryption or compression in a modular, testable way. Implement EncryptionDecorator

# Abstract Decorator

screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember

content.html:
Module 3 › Chapter 3.4 › Key Concepts
Target Interface
The interface the client expects to call.
Adaptee
An existing class with a different interface that needs translation.
Adapter
Implements the target and delegates to the adaptee, translating calls when necessary.
Component
The interface or abstract class that supports decorators and concrete components.
Decorator
A wrapper that conforms to the component interface and adds responsibilities dynamically.
Dynamic Responsibility Assignment

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn two complementary structural patterns that help existing code keep working while your system evolves. First, the Adapter pattern solves the classic problem of incompatible interfaces: it lets client code speak the interface it expects while translating calls to an older or third-party class without modifying that class. Second, the Decorator pattern offers a runtime way to add responsibilities to individual objects, avoiding a combinatorial explosion of subclasses. You will see concrete examples: adapting a legacy payment gateway to a new payment interface and wrapping a simple coffee object with milk and sugar decorators. We'll also cover trade-offs: composition versus inheritance for adapters, and when a decorator is preferable to subclassing. These patterns are practical for integrating legacy systems, extending behavior in deployed code, and composing features at runtime. As you proceed, notice the difference in intent—Adapter changes interfaces, Decorator adds responsibilities—and try to predict which pattern fits small real-world scenarios. What integration problem in your codebase could use an adapter, and where might decorators reduce subclass complexity?

By the end of this chapter you will be able to identify when interfaces are incompatible and apply the Adapter pattern to bridge that gap without modifying existing code. You will also implement object adapters using composition and understand the theoretical idea of class adapters and their trade-offs. Next, you will explain the intent of the Decorator pattern and implement decorators to add responsibilities at runtime in a way that avoids combinatorial subclassing. Finally, you will compare Decorator with inheritance and related wrappers like Proxy or Adapter, and make an informed decision about which approach fits a given problem. Each objective is paired with an actionable milestone, such as writing an adapter from a legacy connector to a new data source interface or layering encryption and compression decorators. These are practical outcomes: you won't only read the pattern names, you'll implement them in code and reason about trade-offs in real integration scenarios.

These next objectives focus on applying patterns and comparing alternatives. You will implement decorators that wrap any component to add functionality such as encryption or compression and test them independently. You will contrast decorator composition with inheritance: use inheritance when every instance must share new behavior at compile time, and prefer decorators when you need per-instance flexibility at runtime. You will also practice combining Adapter and Decorator: adapt a legacy data source to a modern interface and then layer an encryption decorator on top of the adapted source. Finally, you'll gain a habit of asking two questions before choosing a pattern: do I need to change the interface, or add behavior to some instances? Those quick questions will guide you toward Adapter or Decorator and keep your code maintainable as systems evolve.

The Adapter pattern is a structural design pattern whose purpose is to convert the interface of an existing class into another interface the client expects. Imagine a device plug and an outlet socket that don't match: the adapter sits between them and translates the connection. In software, the adapter accepts calls in the target interface, performs any translation or mapping, and delegates the work to the adaptee. This means you do not modify the original adaptee — a crucial advantage when that code is third-party, legacy, or widely reused. A concrete example from this chapter is adapting a legacy payment gateway that expects a legacy currency code to a new payment processor interface that uses currency abbreviations. The adapter maps the currency formats and forwards the call. A common misconception is that an adapter changes the adaptee; it does not. Another confusion is mixing adapters with proxies or decorators; adapters change interface, proxies control access, and decorators add behavior. Key takeaway: use adapters when the interface mismatch, not when you need to change behavior. How would you describe a good translation between two interfaces in your current project?

There are two conceptual forms of adapters: object adapters and class adapters. An object adapter uses composition: it holds an instance of the adaptee and translates calls from the client's expected interface into calls on that internal instance. This form is the most common because it preserves encapsulation and works easily in languages that limit multiple inheritance. A class adapter uses inheritance: the adapter inherits from both the target interface and the adaptee, effectively being both. While class adapters can be concise in languages that support multiple inheritance, they break encapsulation and tightly couple the adapter to the adaptee. A concrete trade-off: object adapters let you swap or mock the adaptee at runtime and make testing easier; class adapters bake the adaptee's behavior into the adapter and are harder to change. A common misunderstanding is to assume class adapters always require language-level multiple inheritance; think of them conceptually but implement with composition when multiple inheritance is not practical. Key takeaway: prefer composition for flexibility and testability unless you have a compelling reason and language support for class adapters. Object Adapter vs Class Adapter means object adapters favor flexibility and encapsulation; class adapters can be simpler conceptually but increase coupling.. In practical terms, trade-offs between composition and inheritance. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's walk through the object adapter example from the chapter to make the idea concrete. The client expects a NewPaymentProcessor with a make payment method that accepts an amount and a currency abbreviation such as USD. The existing class, OldPaymentGateway, exposes process payment legacy and expects an amount and a legacy numeric currency code. The adapter implements the NewPaymentProcessor interface and holds an OldPaymentGateway instance. When make payment is called, the adapter maps the readable currency abbreviation to the legacy code, perhaps using a small dictionary, and calls process payment legacy on the adaptee. This preserves the old gateway's behavior and avoids touching its source. A practical pitfall is to leak adapter mapping logic across the codebase; keep translation logic within the adapter. Another misconception is treating adapters as feature enhancers; they should focus on translation. Example: the adapter maps USD to 840 and returns whatever the adaptee returns, allowing the client to remain unaware of legacy formats. Takeaway: test adapters with both real and mocked adaptees to ensure translations are correct and edge cases like unknown currencies are handled predictably.

The Decorator pattern is a structural pattern that lets you attach new responsibilities to objects at runtime by wrapping them in decorator objects that conform to the same interface. This approach avoids creating many specialized subclasses for each combination of features. Think of a simple coffee object that has base cost and description; rather than creating subclasses for every topping combination, you wrap the base coffee in a milk decorator, then wrap that in a sugar decorator, and so on. Each decorator delegates to its wrapped component for core behavior and augments cost or description as needed. A common misconception is that decorators are identical to proxies or adapters. While all three use wrapping, their intent differs: decorator focuses on behavior addition, adapter focuses on interface translation, and proxy focuses on controlling access. Example: adding encryption to a data source by wrapping it in an EncryptionDecorator transforms returned data without changing the underlying data source. Takeaway: use decorators when you need per-instance, composable features rather than global class-wide behavior. What is the Decorator pattern? means decorator wraps a component to add responsibilities while preserving the component's public interface.. In practical terms, add responsibilities to objects dynamically without subclassing. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Designing decorators follows a practical sequence. First, define a component interface that lists the operations clients use. Second, implement one or more concrete components that provide the base behavior. Third, create an abstract decorator that implements the component interface and holds a reference to another component. This decorator forwards calls to the wrapped component. Fourth, implement concrete decorators that override or extend specific methods, delegating to the wrapped component and then adding responsibilities such as encryption, compression, or UI enhancements. A concrete example: start with a FileDataSource that reads text from a file, then create an EncryptionDecorator that wraps any DataSource, obtains its data, transforms it by reversing the string to simulate encryption, and returns the transformed text. Important practice: keep decorators single-purpose and composable so they can be layered and tested independently. A misconception to avoid is putting too much logic into a decorator; prefer multiple small decorators instead of one large one. Takeaway: follow the small, composable steps and test each decorator in isolation and in combination. Decorator Implementation Steps means define component, implement base, create abstract decorator, add small single-purpose decorators and layer them.. In practical terms, how to design and layer decorators safely. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Let's examine the decorator structure in action with the coffee and data source examples from the chapter. Start with a SimpleCoffee that returns a base cost and description. The CoffeeDecorator wraps a Coffee instance and delegates calls to it. Concrete decorators such as MilkDecorator and SugarDecorator call the wrapped object's get cost and get description, then add their own cost and description fragments. When you compose decorators, the call chain flows from outermost decorator through inner decorators to the concrete component, accumulating cost and description on the return path. For data sources, FileDataSource reads raw text, DataSourceDecorator forwards get data calls, and EncryptionDecorator wraps a DataSource and returns a transformed value, for example by reversing the string to simulate encryption. A misconception is that decorators must be ordered in a single way; the order affects behavior, so document expected stacking and test different orders. Example scenario: wrap a FileDataSource first with CompressionDecorator then with EncryptionDecorator to compress first and encrypt the compressed payload. Final takeaway: testing both individual decorators and combinations ensures predictable composed behavior at runtime. Let's reinforce three compact ideas from this chapter. First, the Adapter pattern converts one interface into another the client expects, letting you reuse legacy or third-party code without modification. Second, the Decorator pattern wraps components to add responsibilities at runtime, enabling per-instance feature composition and avoiding class combinatorics. Third, the decision rule: if you need to change the shape of the A P I, use an Adapter; if you need to add or vary behavior for particular instances, use a Decorator. Keep adapters focused on translation and decorators focused on behavior. These concepts help you integrate systems and extend features safely while keeping codebase complexity manageable. Here are six compact definitions and reminders to keep at hand. Target Interface: the A P I your client code expects. Adaptee: the existing class with an incompatible interface. Adapter: a translator that implements the target and delegates to the adaptee. Component and Concrete Component: the base interface and an implementation subject to extension. Decorator and Concrete Decorator: a wrapper that conforms to the component interface and adds responsibilities. Dynamic Responsibility Assignment: the core benefit of decorators, enabling features to be added or removed from individual instances at runtime. Keep these terms close when you design: they help you describe intent, explain designs to teammates, and map real problems to the right pattern quickly.
